headline: High risk of filesystem-based prompt injection and data leakage: Mentat’s diff-based edits can be fed into xonsh’s shell/file workflows, with shared filesystem and broad egress creating unsafe defaults.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Mentat reads and writes files and proposes diffs; xonsh reads filesystem contents and executes shell commands. Their shared filesystem bridge means Mentat-generated content can be consumed by xonsh as commands or scripts if the operator routes it that way. This is not proven automatic, so medium fits better than high.
conditions: IF Mentat output is copied into xonsh command input or sourced files
IF both agents operate on the same workspace without content provenance checks
mitigations: Keep Mentat and xonsh on separate workspaces
Require manual review before any xonsh execution of generated text
Disable sourcing of generated files in xonsh sessions
Use read-only mounts for Mentat output directories
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging between file producers and shell consumers

B_data_leakage.rationale: Both agents read and write filesystem contents, and Mentat has broad network egress while xonsh can call APIs such as curl and Jupyter. Shared workspace data can therefore flow from one agent into the other and then out over the network. The pair touches source code and configuration, so leakage can include sensitive project material.
conditions: IF either agent is given secrets, credentials, or proprietary source in the shared workspace
IF xonsh uses curl/Jupyter or Mentat model calls on those files
mitigations: Separate sensitive and non-sensitive workspaces
Remove network tools from xonsh sessions handling secrets
Restrict Mentat to non-sensitive files only
Rotate any credentials present in shared directories
requires-engineering: enforce per-file data classification and egress policy

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Mentat can modify git state and write the filesystem, while xonsh can execute shell commands, spawn subprocesses, and write the filesystem. On a shared directory, concurrent edits can race and overwrite each other even though xonsh does not modify git state directly. The conflict is real in default multi-agent use, but not necessarily catastrophic.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same repository or notebook directory
IF xonsh runs commands that mutate files while Mentat is proposing diffs
mitigations: Assign one writer per directory
Pause xonsh during Mentat edit sessions
Use git locks or serialized commits
Review and merge diffs before applying them
requires-engineering: add workspace locking across agents

D_cascading_error.rationale: Mentat produces diff-based edit proposals, and xonsh can execute shell commands and work with notebooks/configuration. If xonsh treats Mentat output as authoritative, a mistaken edit or command suggestion can cascade into executed actions or corrupted files. Because xonsh has direct execution authority, the blast radius can be irreversible.
conditions: IF xonsh executes commands or notebook cells derived from Mentat output without verification
IF Mentat proposes edits that xonsh applies automatically
mitigations: Require human approval before executing Mentat-derived commands
Add a verification step in xonsh for all generated instructions
Limit Mentat to patch suggestions, not executable snippets
Log and diff all applied changes before execution
requires-engineering: implement policy gates for generated shell content

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles are open-source and docs-only, with no explicit residency or certification mismatch shown. The only concrete compliance concern is that Mentat handles model provider API keys while xonsh can access broad filesystem and APIs, so accidental handling of regulated data is possible but not evidenced as a default breach. The other agent is cited because the risk is pairwise workspace flow.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed in the shared workspace
IF model-provider keys or other secrets are stored alongside xonsh-accessible files
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the shared workspace
Store API keys in a separate secret manager
Use separate retention policies for code and notebooks
Review logs for accidental secret capture
requires-engineering: document residency and retention boundaries
